title: What is cloud computing
fallback_explanation: Cloud computing means renting computing power, storage and software over the internet instead of owning your own servers. Think of a matatu. You do not buy a bus for every trip you take; you pay for a seat when you need to travel. Cloud services work the same way: you use what you need, when you need it, and the provider keeps the vehicles running.

title: Benefits of the cloud (scalability, elasticity, reliability)
fallback_explanation: Cloud benefits include scalability, which means growing resources to handle more users, elasticity, which means adding or removing capacity automatically as demand changes, and reliability, which means services keep running even when parts fail. Picture a juice seller at a busy Saturday market. She sets up more stalls when the crowd grows and packs some away when it quietens down, so her customers keep getting served.

title: CapEx vs OpEx and consumption-based pricing
fallback_explanation: CapEx is money spent up front on assets you own, like buying a generator for your shop. OpEx is money spent on services as you use them, like buying airtime or prepaid electricity tokens. Consumption-based pricing in the cloud follows the OpEx idea: you pay for the units you actually use, such as compute hours or storage, so you avoid a large upfront purchase and can stop paying when you stop using the service.

title: Shared responsibility model
fallback_explanation: In the shared responsibility model, the cloud provider and the customer each look after different parts of the service. Think of a shop in a market. The landlord maintains the building, the roof and the security gate. The shopkeeper locks the shop, guards the stock and manages who has keys. In cloud services the provider protects the physical datacentre and underlying hardware, while the customer protects its own data, user access and settings.

title: Public, private and hybrid cloud
fallback_explanation: A public cloud is shared infrastructure run by a provider and available to many customers, like a shared matatu stage that serves everyone. A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation, like a family car that only the family uses. A hybrid cloud combines both, much like a family that uses its own car for school runs and matatus for longer journeys. Each model suits different needs for cost, control and compliance.

title: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
fallback_explanation: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS describe how much of the stack the provider manages. With IaaS you rent the basics, like virtual machines and storage, and manage the operating system and apps yourself, similar to renting an empty plot and bringing your own cooking equipment. With PaaS the provider also runs the platform, so you focus on your code, like renting a fully equipped kitchen. With SaaS you simply use a finished application, like buying ready-made mandazi from a vendor.

title: Regions and availability zones
fallback_explanation: A region is a geographic area with one or more datacentres, such as a whole country or a cluster of cities. An availability zone is a physically separate datacentre inside a region, with its own power and cooling. Think of a family that keeps copies of important documents in two different houses in the same town. If one house floods, the other is still safe. Spreading resources across zones helps services stay available when one site has a problem.

title: Resource groups and subscriptions
fallback_explanation: A subscription is a billing and access boundary in Azure. A resource group is a container that holds related resources, such as the virtual machines and storage for one app. Think of a school with its own budget, where each classroom holds the desks and books for one class. Resource groups let you manage, update or delete related items together. Subscriptions help you separate costs and permissions between teams or projects.

title: Virtual machines and scale sets
fallback_explanation: A virtual machine is a software computer running in an Azure datacentre, which you can size to suit your workload. A scale set runs a group of identical virtual machines and adds or removes them automatically as demand changes. Think of a bakery that hires more bakers on busy Fridays and sends some home on quiet mornings. You pay for the machines while they run, so scaling helps match cost to demand.

title: App Service and containers
fallback_explanation: App Service is a managed platform for running web apps and APIs, so you do not have to manage the underlying servers. A container packages an app with everything it needs so it runs the same way anywhere. Think of a cook who rents a ready-built kiosk with water and power instead of building one. The kiosk is like App Service. The sealed lunchbox that carries the same meal anywhere is like a container. Both let developers focus on the food, not the building.

title: Storage accounts and redundancy
fallback_explanation: A storage account groups Azure storage services such as blobs, files, queues and tables under one namespace. Redundancy keeps extra copies of your data so it survives failures. Locally redundant storage keeps copies within one datacentre, while zone and geo redundant options keep copies in other zones or regions. Think of a market trader who keeps stock in one stall, or splits it between a home and a second store in another town. More copies cost more, so choose the level that matches how important the data is.

title: Virtual networks and VPN
fallback_explanation: An Azure virtual network, or VNet, is a private network in the cloud where your resources can communicate securely. A VPN connects your on-premises network to Azure over an encrypted tunnel across the internet. Think of a company with offices in two towns. The public road is shared with everyone, but a private, secured route links the head office and the branch. The VPN keeps traffic private even though it travels over public infrastructure.

title: Microsoft Entra ID and authentication
fallback_explanation: Microsoft Entra ID is Azure's cloud-based identity service. It manages user accounts and controls how people sign in. Authentication proves who you are, usually with a password, a code or another factor. Authorisation decides what you are allowed to do, which is handled separately. Think of a shop assistant who checks an ID card and a staff badge before letting someone into a store room. Checking identity first means the right people reach the right resources.

title: Zero trust and defence in depth
fallback_explanation: Zero trust is a security approach that does not automatically trust any user or device, so every access request is checked. Defence in depth means using several layers of protection, so one failed layer does not expose everything. Think of a home with a locked gate, a locked door, a locked cupboard, and a visitor who is still checked inside the compound. No single lock has to be perfect, because each check adds protection. Zero trust applies the same idea: verify every request and limit what each user can reach.

title: Cost management and the pricing calculator
fallback_explanation: Cost management in Azure helps you estimate, track and control spending using cost analysis, budgets and alerts. The pricing calculator lets you estimate costs before you deploy anything. Think of planning a family budget for a school term. You estimate fees and supplies before paying, then check spending against the plan each month. Estimating first helps avoid surprises on the bill. Prices vary by service, region and usage, so always check current figures on the official calculator.

title: Tags, Azure Policy and resource locks
fallback_explanation: Tags are name and value labels, such as department equals finance, that help you organise and report on resources. Azure Policy checks resources against rules, such as allowing only certain regions, and can audit or block non-compliant ones. A resource lock helps prevent accidental deletion or changes. Think of a shop that labels its stock, allows only approved suppliers to stock its shelves, and keeps the cash box padlocked. Each tool protects or organises resources in a different way.

title: Role-based access control (RBAC)
fallback_explanation: Role-based access control, or RBAC, decides who can do what on Azure resources. It assigns roles at a scope such as a subscription or resource group. A role is a set of permissions, such as reader or contributor. Think of a school where teachers can enter marks, the bursar can see fee records, and visitors can only walk the grounds. Giving people the smallest role they need reduces risk. RBAC controls actions, and it is separate from how users sign in.

title: Azure Monitor and Service Health
fallback_explanation: Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs from your resources so you can see performance, trends and alerts. Azure Service Health shows issues that affect Azure services in your regions, such as planned maintenance or outages. Think of a matatu SACCO that tracks its own trips and fuel records, and also receives notices when a road is closed. Monitor shows what is happening in your own resources. Service Health reports on the health of the platform itself.

title: Azure Resource Manager, CLI and PowerShell
fallback_explanation: Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management layer that Azure tools use to create, update and delete resources. The Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell are command-line tools that send requests to Resource Manager, so you can script tasks. Think of a government office where every request, whether made in person, by phone or by letter, goes through one front desk that records it. The front desk is like Resource Manager, and the different ways of asking are like the portal, CLI and PowerShell.

title: Microsoft Purview and compliance
fallback_explanation: Microsoft Purview is the Azure service for data governance and compliance. It helps organisations discover, classify and manage their data, which supports compliance with rules and standards. Think of a school records office that knows where every student file is kept and who is allowed to see each one. Purview does not make an organisation compliant on its own. It gives visibility and controls, and the organisation still has to meet its own legal and regulatory duties.
